subject: ventures/ticket-resale-profit-calculator
professional: a full-time ticket broker and the accountant who does their books; they check first that the break-even list price after the seller fee is right to the cent, that the fee presets match what each marketplace actually keeps, and that a season's sales log in their own column names gives the profit and ROI their bank deposits show

evidence.correctness: Price engine recomputed by hand on three CLI runs (2x$120 at $150/10%/80%; 15% target-profit; 4x$85.50 with flat fee, delivery and salvage --json) and the 12-row worked log recomputed in Python: every figure matched to the cent. The log parser gives wrong numbers on plausible headers: 'Net Profit' before 'Payout' turns +$70 into -$130; 'Cost per ticket' turns 35% ROI into 170%; blank fees become 0. Wrong silent numbers on realistic input cap this at 2.
evidence.completeness: Every claimed feature ran end to end in the CLI: price, break-even, target profit, four-marketplace comparison, expected profit with salvage, log by platform, losing sales, --min-roi exit 1, stdin, --json, exit 2 on bad input. Gaps: 'Sold On' and 'Buyer' headers make every row unreadable; salvage above payout prints 'n/a'. The served page could not be loaded (proxy 403).
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs': 31 pass, 0 fail. Five seeded mutations via quality_mutate.py: only the Ticketmaster preset change was caught; flat fee in break-even (engine.mjs:60), salvage in break-even p (79), delivery in effective fee (52) and the 'net' payout alias (115) all survived.
evidence.craft: engine.mjs (202 lines), cli.mjs, index.html script read. Small, pure, zero-dependency, input validation with RangeError and exit 2. Defects: prefix-matching header regexes with first-match column assignment and no exclusion (engine.mjs:108-149), silent $0 fallback for a missing fee (157), summary string money formatting (194).
evidence.claims: Disclaimer, privacy, local usage counting with opt-out present on both pages. Guide arithmetic (11% above cost, 89 in 100, a quarter margin, 12% at 4 in 5) all hold by hand. Tax line is hedged and consistent with IRS IR-2025-107 ($20,000/200 1099-K). Fee presets fall in the third-party 2025 range but carry no source or date. INPUT_NOTES 'not guessed' is contradicted by the blank-fee fallback and header misreads.
evidence.fitness: Professional: a full-time ticket broker (and their accountant). Pricing one listing works and the expected-profit line is the right first question. Auditing a season needs a hand-built CSV with lot cost (marketplace exports have neither cost nor these headers), and a broker's own column names ('Net Profit', 'Cost per ticket', 'Sold On') are the ones misread. No per-ticket cost, sale date, partial sell-through or tax-year view.
evidence.domain: Break-even = (cost + flat + delivery)/(qty(1-fee)) and break-even p = (cost - salvage)/(payout - salvage) are the correct formulas. Departures from broker practice: binary all-or-nothing sale with no markdown ladder or partial sell-through, cross-platform comparison at one list price (buyer-fee and all-in pricing differences acknowledged in the guide), uncited presets, no payout-method fees, and no note that casual-seller losses are not deductible.

defects.what: Sales-log header regexes match by prefix and columns are claimed first-match with no exclusion, so plausible headers give silently wrong numbers: a 'Net Profit' column before 'Payout' is read as the payout ($70 profit reported as a $130 loss, -65% ROI), and 'Cost per ticket' is read as the lot cost (35% ROI reported as 170%).
'Sold On', which the platform regex lists as an alias, also matches the sale regex ^sold, and any 'Buyer' column matches cost ^buy; either makes every row unreadable ('No sales rows could be read').

A blank or unreadable fees cell with no payout column is taken as $0 fees, so payout = gross and profit is overstated with '0% of gross went to fees'; INPUT_NOTES says unreadable rows are skipped, not guessed.

Four of five seeded mutations survive the 31 tests: dropping the flat fee from the break-even/target price, dropping salvage from the break-even sale chance, dropping delivery from the effective fee rate, and removing the 'net' payout alias. No test asserts listForProfit or breakEvenPSell with a flat fee or salvage, or any header other than the canonical names.

Fee presets (10/10/10/15%) carry no source or check date in code, README or page ('as last checked'). They sit inside the range third-party 2025 sources give (NITO NY report: 10% for StubHub, SeatGeek, Vivid Seats), but StubHub is often quoted at 15% and Ticketmaster does not publish a rate.

When salvage is worth at least the payout the CLI prints 'needs n/a to break even' rather than saying selling never beats holding; summary text prints '$-130' and '$4730' without sign-first or two-decimal formatting.

Scope: the log nets losing sales against winners in one profit figure; for a casual seller a loss on personal-use tickets is not deductible while a gain is, and a dealer reports Schedule C income with SE tax. No note tells the user the log total is not a taxable figure, and the log has no per-ticket cost, sale date or 1099-K reconciliation a broker's accountant asks for first.

verdict: The pricing engine is right: break-even, target-profit price, payout, ROI, effective fee rate, expected profit with salvage and the break-even sale chance all matched hand recomputation to the cent on three CLI runs, and the 12-sale worked log matched an independent Python recompute. The guide's arithmetic holds and the tax wording agrees with the IRS's 2025 1099-K rule. It does not meet the bar. The sales-log parser matches header names by prefix and takes the first match, so a 'Net Profit' column becomes the payout (a $70 gain reported as a $130 loss) and 'Cost per ticket' becomes the lot cost (35% ROI shown as 170%), with no warning; 'Sold On' and 'Buyer' columns make every row unreadable; a blank fee is silently $0. Four of five seeded mutations survive the 31 tests, including dropping the flat fee from the break-even price. The fee presets sit within 2025 third-party ranges but cite no source or date. Completeness 3; correctness, craft, claims, fitness and domain 2; verification 1.
